raw_response:
I farm only 6 mu, so I cannot afford to gamble too much. I have done wheat-maize for many years, and on land like mine in Quzhou this is still the safest way: wheat gives one harvest, maize gives the next, and if one side is weaker I still have the other. I finished middle school, so I do pay attention to what the extension people say, but I do not follow it exactly by the book. I usually look at what worked on my own field and compare with the better farmers nearby. Last year, wheat responded well when I split the fertilizer instead of putting too much at once, and maize did better when I seeded quickly right after wheat harvest. So this year I will keep the same basic pattern, not too light on fertilizer because I do not want to lose yield, but not so heavy that I waste cash. Water from the well helps, but pumping costs money, so I will irrigate at the key stages, not blindly.

For wheat, I will sow in early October with an improved local variety that people around here commonly use, not the most expensive seed. I will prepare the land with normal rotary tillage after the maize comes off, put base fertilizer down first, and then topdress around jointing if the crop looks like it can carry yield. Wheat is my more reliable crop, so I am willing to give it three irrigations if the season is dry enough. For maize, the main thing is speed after wheat harvest. The window is tight, so I will not do heavy tillage; I will clear the wheat and get maize in quickly, using hybrid seed because maize seed quality matters more. I will feed maize mainly at planting and then again around the big bell stage. If summer rain is normal, one irrigation may be enough; if it turns dry, I can add another because I have the well. Most labor will still be from the family, and I will only spend on hired service where timing matters.
